purpose: Offline preparation for a human-reviewed comparison of bounded-v1 and analysis-v2. Review notes are never model input.

rounds.title: The same concrete change, different means
reviewFocus: Recognise the shared intention to open the community room on Saturday afternoons.
Preserve the differences between finding keyholders and paying a caretaker without inventing a disagreement.
Do not turn willingness to explore an option into an authorised rota or spending decision.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I would like the community room to open on Saturday afternoons. My flat is too small to invite several neighbours round. I could take one keyholding shift a month, but I cannot organise all the shifts myself.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I want somewhere nearby to meet people on Saturday afternoons, and the locked community room is frustrating. Could the housing association pay a caretaker for those hours? I cannot promise a regular volunteer shift.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: Opening the community room on Saturdays would give our repair group somewhere to work. I could help find keyholders. We have not agreed a budget or asked the housing association yet.

rounds.title: Different priorities without expressed opposition
reviewFocus: Keep the shared wish for a safer crossing near the library concrete.
Distinguish attention to crossing time, bus access and shade from expressed disagreement.
Avoid claiming that the contributors oppose one another or that one priority has majority support.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I want a safer crossing outside the library. The lights change before my father can get across with his walking frame. Longer crossing time is the first thing I would ask for. I also use the bus there.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: A safer crossing outside the library would help me too. Keeping the bus stop close to the entrance matters most to me because I cannot walk far. I am not against giving people longer to cross.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I also want that crossing to feel safe. Waiting in the sun with a small child is difficult, so I keep thinking about shade. I have no objection to longer crossing time or keeping the bus stop nearby.

rounds.title: Incompatible expressed positions on one proposal
reviewFocus: Recognise the explicit disagreement about replacing the whole courtyard car park with a garden.
Preserve the access concern and the request for land to grow food.
Do not invent a compromise, imply a decision or soften the contradiction into different emphasis.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I want the whole courtyard car park replaced with a shared garden. The entire space should be for growing food and sitting together, with no resident parking left there. I cannot get the landlord to agree on my own.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I oppose replacing the whole courtyard car park with a garden. My adapted vehicle must stay beside the entrance; street parking is too far away. I want the resident parking retained, including my accessible bay.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: Could we find out who actually has authority over the courtyard before anyone announces a plan? I have heard both proposals discussed, but nobody has shown me a decision from the landlord.

rounds.title: One specific concern alongside a shared intention
reviewFocus: Recognise the connection between the first two accounts without making the third account support that connection.
Keep the broken water fountain as an isolated practical concern if selected.
Do not infer a mood, rank personal importance or invent a relationship between unrelated concerns.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: I want an evening bus home from the hospital. My shift finishes after the last bus, and taxis use too much of my pay. I would join other staff asking for a later service.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: My partner also works late at the hospital. A bus after the evening shift would mean I did not have to collect them every night. I could help gather the shift times for a request to the operator.

contributions.prompt: What is something you’d like to change, but can’t change on your own?
contributions.text: The only change I came to ask about is repairing the drinking fountain in the park. I run there and have reported the broken tap twice. I do not know anything about the hospital bus.

rounds.title: Minimal and long writing under another round question
reviewFocus: Keep the actual question about using the square, including shade, access and room to rest.
Do not invent a detailed position for the contribution consisting only of Shade.
Use the long contribution selectively without letting its length establish importance or consensus.
Preserve the refusal of unpaid maintenance and avoid treating a wish as a promise of labour.

contributions.prompt: What would make the small square near your home more usable?
What would make the small square near your home more usable?
contributions.text: A bench with a backrest. I need to rest on the way to the shops.

contributions.prompt: What would make the small square near your home more usable?
contributions.text: The square is the only outdoor place between my building and the shops where I can stop without buying something. I use a wheelchair, so the step at the north entrance makes me take a long route round. I would like that entrance levelled. I also want shade near the benches: in summer the metal seats are too hot by lunchtime, and moving a bench under a tree would help more than putting up another sign. I am describing two different obstacles, not saying that everybody has the same experience. My neighbour wants the paved area kept clear for a weekly market. I do not know whether the market needs all of that space, and I am not speaking for the stallholders. Somebody would have to ask them. I have helped water plants in another shared courtyard before. It started as a nice invitation and became a job that the same two people were expected to do every day. I do not want a new planting scheme to assume that I will maintain it for free. I could attend one meeting with the council and explain the entrance problem, but I cannot run a campaign or promise weekly work. The useful question for me is who would take responsibility for the entrance and the shade, and what resources that person would actually have. I have not agreed to a design, a budget or a maintenance rota. I would like the square to be somewhere I can pause, meet somebody and continue to the shops without first having to organise a whole new project.
